name: Carlos Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run nine hundred ewes on Crag End, which is six hundred hectares of hill, most of it rough grazing and bracken, plus some better fields down by the river. In November the rams are in with the ewes, so every morning I'm on the quad bike with the dogs, Bess and Moss, checking the rams are working and nobody's stuck in a ditch. Then it's feeding, fencing, and a lot of looking at the sky.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the gather, that's when we bring all the sheep down off the hill together, three or four of us and a dozen dogs. On a good day in September, with the light on the tops, there's no better job in the world. What wears me out is lambing in April, three weeks of two hours' sleep a night, and the price of lamb, which never seems to match the work.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who else is on the farm?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Ruth is a district nurse, so she's out all day visiting patients. My nephew Kwame works with me four days a week, he's thirty and good with dogs. At the gather, the neighbours come and I go to theirs. That's how it works up here.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any technology or AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The sheep have electronic ear tags now, by law, and I've got a reader that logs weights. I held out until most of the valley had one, then I bought one second-hand. I've used one of those AI chat things a couple of times, to fill in a grant form. It was decent at it, better than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's fine. Useful for forms, and the rest is farming as usual. At the mart, that's the livestock market, I'd say the same as everyone: lamb prices are the problem, not computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it changes nothing. The hill doesn't care. If anything I'd use it a bit more for the paperwork, which is the bit of the job I hate most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The usual. I'd re-fence the top boundary, about two kilometres, maybe five thousand with a grant covering half. I'd buy a young dog to bring on, because Bess is nine. I'd use the AI for the grant form again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pleased, even, if it takes the forms off my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about buying a young dog. What does that involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You go to a trial or a breeder you trust, and you watch the parents work. A good pup is maybe a thousand, a trained one five or six. I'd rather a pup and train it myself over two years. Bess was a pup from Iolo's old collie, Nell, and she's the best dog I've had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said lamb prices are the problem. What would you change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, really. Some years it's the supermarkets, some years it's imports, some years it's people eating less lamb. I'm not one for blaming one thing. I'd just like the price to cover the cost of a ewe for a year, which some years it doesn't.

S0.say: I'd say AI is fine and useful for forms, and the rest is farming as usual. At the livestock market I'd say lamb prices are the real problem.
S0.think: Privately it changes nothing for me, because the hill doesn't care. I'd just use it more for the paperwork I hate.
S0.do: Re-fences two kilometres of the top boundary for about five thousand, half from a grant. Buys a pup to train up because Bess is nine, and uses AI for the grant form.
S0.feel: Calm, even pleased if it takes the forms off his hands.
S0.quote: Bess was a pup from Iolo's old collie, Nell, and she's the best dog I've had.
S0.fieldNote: Steady and unbothered, with a clear rhythm of farming life. He refuses to pin blame on any single cause, which fits his middle-ground views. His affection for the dogs is the warmest note of the opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Second picture. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it sounds reasonable, giving everyone time to catch up. I'd also say it's hard on youngsters if companies stop hiring them, and farming can't take them all. But I wouldn't make a speech about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm all right. Hill farming is about as far from AI as you can get. The question is Kwame, because he'll want his own farm one day, and young people already struggle to get a tenancy up here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Kwame about a share-farming deal, where he owns part of the flock and takes part of the profit, so he's building something. I'd give him two hundred ewes to start, worth maybe thirty thousand. I'd also let him try any new tool that comes along before I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with some thinking about the next generation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd let Kwame try new tools first. Why him first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if it's rubbish, he'll find out quickly and I won't have wasted money. And if it's good, he'll show me, and I'll listen to him more than a salesman. That's how I got the ear tag reader. Kwame used his friend's for a week and said, Uncle, get one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two hundred ewes is a big gift. What would Ruth say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth would say it's about time. Neither of our kids wants the farm, our daughter's a vet in the city. Kwame is the nearest we've got to a successor. Better he builds his stake while I'm still on my feet.

S1.say: I'd say slow change sounds reasonable and gives everyone time. It's hard on youngsters if companies stop hiring them, but I wouldn't make a speech about it.
S1.think: Privately I'm all right, since hill farming is far from AI. My concern is my nephew Kwame, who'll want his own farm when tenancies are already scarce.
S1.do: Offers Kwame a share-farming deal starting with two hundred ewes, worth about thirty thousand, so he builds his own stake. Lets Kwame test any new tool first.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, thinking about the next generation.
S1.quote: Kwame used his friend's for a week and said, Uncle, get one.
S1.fieldNote: He shows what steady adaptability looks like in practice: wait, let someone you trust test it, then adopt. Kwame is both his successor and his scout. Succession planning is quiet but concrete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's rough for office people, and the government should do something sensible, not just shout. Retraining, help with bills while people find their feet. I'd say that, and then I'd go back to the sheep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, for me it's mostly the paperwork side. The agency that runs our farm payments would be run by these assistants, and if they get it wrong, who do I ring? Last year a payment came two months late, and it took a real person on the phone to fix it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep paper copies of everything, every form, every receipt, in the box file in the kitchen. I'd use the AI tools a bit more myself, so I understand what they do. And I'd keep three months' costs in the bank instead of spending it on the shed roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for the sheep, but for dealing with the office side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened with that late payment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The system said a field was the wrong size, by half a hectare, and it froze the whole payment. Eleven thousand pounds. I rang for three weeks until a woman called Sandra looked at a map and said, oh, that's obviously wrong, and fixed it in ten minutes. If Sandra's replaced by a machine, I don't know what I'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ruth's a nurse. Does this picture touch her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not her job, no, you can't do a dressing over the internet. But the scheduling and the records, maybe. She says half her day is typing already. If a machine did the typing, she might actually like it, she'd see more patients.

S2.say: I'd say it's rough for office people and the government should do something sensible like retraining and help with bills, not just shout.
S2.think: Privately my worry is the farm payments agency being run by AI assistants. When a payment went wrong last year, only a real person on the phone could fix it.
S2.do: Keeps paper copies of every form and receipt in a kitchen box file and uses AI tools a bit more to understand them. Holds three months' costs in the bank instead of fixing the shed roof.
S2.feel: Uneasy about dealing with the office side of farming.
S2.quote: I rang for three weeks until a woman called Sandra looked at a map and said, oh, that's obviously wrong, and fixed it in ten minutes.
S2.fieldNote: He sees office automation through his dealings with the payments agency, not through jobs. The Sandra story is his evidence that human judgment rescues mistakes. He also sees a possible upside for Ruth, which is a fair-minded touch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Fourth picture. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there has to be a fair deal, and both sides will have to give a bit. I don't trust the people shouting loudest on either side. I'd vote for whoever looked like they'd actually fix it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, house prices booming is bad news up here. Every cottage in the valley becomes a holiday home for someone who made a fortune in shares, and the young people can't afford to live near the farm. Kwame rents a cottage in the village, and his landlord would sell in a heartbeat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do up the old farm cottage, which is half derelict, so Kwame has somewhere to live on the farm. It would cost maybe forty thousand, and I'd need a loan for most of it. I'd also talk to the neighbours about keeping the gather going, because if people sell up, there's nobody to help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. The hill is fine. It's the people on it I'd worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A forty-thousand loan is big at fifty-eight. Would you really take it on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would, actually, if the alternative was Kwame leaving. Without him, I can't run nine hundred ewes. With him, the farm has a future. The loan's a risk, but losing him is a bigger one. I'd talk to the bank in January, before lambing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the gather needs neighbours. What happens if they sell up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then you can't gather. You need six or seven people and their dogs on a hill this size. If two farms become holiday homes, the sheep stay out on the hill longer, and we lose some. That's how hill farming ends, not with a bang, just fewer people at the gather each year.

S3.say: I'd say there has to be a fair deal and both sides will have to give a bit. I'd vote for whoever looked like they'd actually fix it.
S3.think: Privately the house price boom is bad news up here, because valley cottages become holiday homes. Kwame rents in the village, and his landlord would sell in a heartbeat.
S3.do: Takes out a loan of about forty thousand to rebuild the derelict farm cottage for Kwame, talking to the bank in January. Talks with neighbours about keeping the gather going if others sell up.
S3.feel: Anxious, not for the hill but for the people on it.
S3.quote: That's how hill farming ends, not with a bang, just fewer people at the gather each year.
S3.fieldNote: The fast picture threatens him through housing, not work. He's willing to take a big loan late in life to keep his nephew close, which is a real risk for a steady person. His fear is about the shared labour of the gather, the community that makes hill farming possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'd believe it when I see it. Robots on flat farms, maybe. On a hill in sleet, I've got my doubts. But I'd say we should be ready, and that small farms need help to keep up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm torn. A robot dog might gather sheep on a flat field. Up on our hill in sleet, I'd like to see it find the ewe stuck in the bracken. But the things like feeding and checking, drones could do those, and that's a lot of what Kwame does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a year and watch the neighbours. If Iolo or one of the big lowland farms tried a robot that worked on rough ground, I'd go and look. I'd make sure Kwame has the share-farming deal locked in, so he's an owner, not just a worker. And I'd buy a drone for checking the hill, which I've been meaning to do anyway, about two thousand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not panicked. Hill land has always been hard to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the robots did work on the hill, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd buy one, probably second-hand, like the ear tag reader. And Kwame would run it. But I'd still keep the dogs, at least while I'm alive. You don't sell your best friend because a machine came out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would lose out most up here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shearing gangs, probably, and the contractors who come for the hay. If a machine can shear, those lads are done. Some of them are the best workers I know. That would be a real loss for the valley.

S4.say: I'd say I'd believe it when I see it, because hills in sleet are hard for machines. We should be ready, though, and small farms need help to keep up.
S4.think: Privately I'm torn: I doubt robots could find a ewe stuck in bracken, but drones could do the feeding and checking that's much of Kwame's work.
S4.do: Waits a year to watch neighbours try robots on rough ground and locks in Kwame's share-farming deal so he's an owner. Buys a drone for checking the hill, about two thousand.
S4.feel: Anxious but not panicked, because hill land has always been hard to change.
S4.quote: A robot dog might gather sheep on a flat field. Up on our hill in sleet, I'd like to see it find the ewe stuck in the bracken.
S4.fieldNote: He is the only farmer here who thinks his land itself might protect him. Even so, he moves to secure Kwame as an owner. His real loss in this picture is the shearing gangs and the dogs, both part of the community he values.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, number four, because of the houses. Robots on the hill I can wait out, but if the valley empties and Kwame can't live here, the farm's finished. What would help is some rule that keeps homes for people who work locally, and a loan scheme for farm cottages for young workers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the dogs, and they're half the work. Every farmer up here would tell you the same. Whatever happens with robots, I'd want somebody to keep training dogs, because it's a skill that takes a lifetime and it would go in one generation.

headlineQuote: That's how hill farming ends, not with a bang, just fewer people at the gather each year.
portrait: Carlos Mensah is fifty-eight and runs nine hundred ewes on six hundred hectares of hill at Crag End, working with his nephew Kwame and his dogs Bess and Moss. He's steady and practical, waits for others to test new things, and avoids blaming any one cause. Office automation worries him mostly through the farm payments agency, while the fast picture frightens him because holiday homes could push Kwame out of the valley. He doubts robots could manage the hill in sleet, but he'd still secure Kwame as an owner of part of the flock.
biggestWorry: The fast picture worries him most, because a housing boom could empty the valley and leave Kwame nowhere to live.
whatWouldHelp: Rules keeping homes for local workers and a loan scheme to do up farm cottages for young workers.
